order.subject: ela
order.topic: Making inferences and citing text evidence
order.requests: Quiz: Please write two short passages of your own from my notes (about 250-350 words each): one story and one nonfiction article. Both versions read the same two passages but get different questions. 8-10 multiple choice questions, mostly inference and 'which evidence best supports' questions, then one short constructed response at the end: What can you infer about the character? Use two pieces of evidence. Rubric: A 4-point rubric for the constructed response (claim, evidence, explanation), in kid-friendly words my students can use to self-check. General: My students are 7th graders, many reading a little below grade level, so keep sentences clear. Number the paragraphs in the passages so students can cite them.

notes: Header line: Name / Date / Period blanks, then a plain all-caps title with the version (e.g. THEME QUIZ - Version A).
One short directions line: Read ... carefully. Then answer the questions. Circle the letter of the best answer.
Questions numbered 1), 2) …; choices lettered A)–D) (her own sheets use (1) and a)–d); this is the closest the print layout allows).
Paired items labeled Part A / Part B; Part B always reads: Which detail BEST supports your answer to Part A? (BEST in capitals).
Evidence choices are short paraphrased or quoted details followed by the paragraph number in parentheses.
Prompts point students back to the text: Read paragraph 2 again.
Passage paragraphs are numbered [1], [2], ... so students can cite them.
Ends with SHORT RESPONSE (4 points) and the reminder: Remember C-E-E: Claim, Evidence, Explanation.
Self-check tip she uses: Ask yourself: If this were the ONLY sentence I had, would it prove my answer?
Plain, short sentences for readers a little below grade level; friendly, direct teacher voice.

documents.title: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ
documents.directions: Read both passages carefully. Then answer the questions. Circle the letter of the best answer. Ask yourself: If this were the ONLY sentence I had, would it prove my answer?

sections.heading: Passage 1: Ba-da-bum
sections.directions: [1] Marisol sat at the kitchen table in her black concert shirt. It was only seven o'clock, and the winter concert did not start until ten. She bent down and retied her left shoe. Then she retied her right shoe. Then she checked the left one again.

[2] "Eggs?" Dad asked, sliding a plate toward her. Marisol pushed the eggs around with her fork. She took one small bite of toast and set it back down. Her drumsticks were in her backpack, but she unzipped the front pocket three times to make sure they were still there.

[3] Across the table, her little brother Leo grabbed two spoons. He tapped them on the edge of the table: ba-da-bum, ba-da-bum. It was the same beat Marisol had practiced every night for a month. He looked up at her with a huge grin.
[4] "Leo, stop it!" Marisol snapped. "You're doing it wrong, and it's so loud." Leo's grin disappeared. He set the spoons down slowly and stared at his cereal.

[5] The kitchen got very quiet. Marisol looked at the clock. Then she looked at the photo on the fridge of Abuela waving from an airport. Abuela had landed last night. For two years she had heard about Marisol's drumming on the phone, but today she would finally hear it in person. Under the table, Marisol's fingers drummed on her knee.

[6] Dad poured his coffee and said nothing. Marisol did not say anything either for a long minute. Then she reached into her backpack and pulled out her practice sticks, the old ones with the chipped tips. She slid them across the table to Leo.

[7] "Hold them like this," she said quietly, moving his fingers. "Thumbs on the side. Now try it soft." Leo tapped very gently: ba-da-bum. "That's it," Marisol said. "You can sit in the front row and watch my hands."
[8] Leo hugged the sticks to his chest. Marisol finally picked up her toast and ate the whole piece.

prompt.A: Read paragraph 1 again. Marisol reties her shoes over and over, three hours before the concert. What does this detail suggest?
prompt.B: Read paragraph 2 again. Marisol unzips her backpack pocket three times to look at her drumsticks. What does this detail suggest?

A: Her new shoes do not fit her feet well yet.
She is worried and needs something to keep her busy.
She wants to look neat when Abuela sees her play.
She is excited and eager for the big concert to start soon.
B: She feels proud about her new drumsticks and likes to see them.
She plans to practice her part in the car on the way to the concert.
The zipper on it is broken and keeps getting stuck.
She is anxious about how the concert will go.

why.A: B is right. She reties her shoes over and over, which shows worry and a need to stay busy. A and C are not in the story. D sounds reasonable, but the story shows nerves, not eagerness: she can't eat.
why.B: D is right. Checking the pocket three times shows worry. The story never says the sticks are new or that she is proud of them (A). It says nothing about practicing in the car (B) or a broken zipper (C).

questions.skill: Make an inference about a character (Part A)

prompt.A: Part A: Read paragraph 3. What can you infer about how Leo feels about his sister?
prompt.B: Part A: Read paragraphs 4-6. Why does Marisol go quiet for a long minute after she yells at Leo?

A: He is bored and hopes she will play a game with him.
He wants to bug her by making a lot of noise at the table.
He is jealous of all the attention his sister gets.
He looks up to her and wants to be like her.
B: She feels bad about how she spoke to him.
She wants Dad to scold Leo.
She is thinking hard about how to play her drum solo.
She is too tired to talk after a short night.

why.A: D. Leo copies the exact beat she practiced and grins at her, so he admires her. B is wrong because he grins at her and is upset when she snaps, so he was not trying to annoy her. A and C are not shown. He never asks to play, and nothing shows him wanting her attention for himself.
why.B: A. She just made Leo's grin disappear, and right after the quiet she is kind to him. That shows she feels bad. C is wrong because the quiet comes right after she hurts Leo, and she ends it by helping him, not by practicing. B and D have no support. Dad says nothing, and nothing says she slept badly.

questions.skill: Choose evidence that supports an inference (Part B)

prompt.A: Part B: Which detail BEST supports your answer to Part A?
prompt.B: Part B: Which detail from the story BEST supports your answer to Part A?

A: He taps out the same beat she practiced, then grins at her. (paragraph 3)
Leo grabs two spoons and taps them on the edge of the table. (paragraph 3)
It is seven o'clock, and the concert does not start until ten. (paragraph 1)
Marisol is wearing her black concert shirt for the big day. (paragraph 1)
B: Then the kitchen got very quiet. (paragraph 5)
She glances up at the clock on the wall. (paragraph 5)
She speaks softly and gently moves Leo's fingers into place. (paragraph 7)
Marisol pushes her eggs around and takes one bite of toast. (paragraph 2)

why.A: A. Copying HER beat and grinning at her shows he looks up to her. B tells us only that he makes noise. It could seem to back up 'he wants to bug her,' but it leaves out that the beat is hers. C could seem to back up 'he is bored,' but it is about the time, not Leo. D could seem to back up 'he is jealous,' but it tells us nothing about how Leo feels.
why.B: C is right. Her soft, gentle help shows she feels bad and wants to make it up to Leo. A is true (after she snapped, the kitchen got very quiet), but a quiet room does not show how she feels. B and D show nerves.

questions.skill: Judge which evidence best proves a claim

prompt.A: A classmate says, "Marisol cares about Leo, even when she is stressed." Which detail, if it were the ONLY one you had, would BEST prove this?
prompt.B: A classmate says, "Marisol is nervous because Abuela will hear her play for the first time." Which detail, if it were the ONLY one you had, would BEST prove this?

A: Marisol finally picks up her toast and eats the whole piece. (paragraph 8)
Marisol snaps at Leo and tells him he is doing the beat all wrong. (paragraph 4)
Marisol slides her old practice sticks across to her brother. (paragraph 6)
Marisol's fingers drum on her knee under the table. (paragraph 5)
B: Marisol says Leo can sit in the front row. (paragraph 7)
Right after looking at Abuela's photo, Marisol drums on her knee. (paragraph 5)
Marisol ties and reties both of her shoes. (paragraph 1)
Abuela landed at the airport last night. (paragraph 5)

why.A: C is right. She is still stressed, but she gives Leo her own sticks, so she cares about him. A shows she feels calmer, not that she cares. B shows only stress. D shows only nerves.
why.B: B. This links Abuela to a nervous habit at the same moment, so it proves both parts of the claim. D names Abuela but shows no nerves at all. C shows nerves but says nothing about Abuela. A shows neither.

questions.skill: Why the author included a detail (story)

prompt.A: Why does the author include the photo of Abuela on the fridge in paragraph 5?
prompt.B: Why does the author end the story with Marisol eating the whole piece of toast?

A: To hint at a reason this concert means so much to Marisol.
To show that Marisol misses Abuela and wants her to visit.
To show that Marisol is sad Abuela lives far away.
To describe what the kitchen looks like in the morning.
B: To hint that she is excited for the big day ahead.
To show she is still too nervous to say much to anyone.
To show that Leo has forgiven her after she snapped at him.
To show that she feels calmer after being kind to Leo.

why.A: A is right. Abuela will hear Marisol play in person for the first time, so the concert matters a lot. B and C are wrong because Abuela is already here (she landed last night), and the story never shows Marisol sad about distance. D misses the point.
why.B: D is right. She could not eat before. Now she eats the whole piece after helping Leo, so she is calmer. The story never shows her excited (A). B is the opposite of what happens. C is about Leo, not the toast.

sections.heading: Passage 2: The Crow Next Door
sections.directions: [1] You have probably seen a crow picking through trash or calling from a power line. Many people think of crows as noisy pests. But scientists have found that the crows living in our cities may be some of the smartest animals around.

[2] Crows can remember human faces. In one set of studies, researchers wore a certain mask while they caught a few crows, checked them, and let them go unharmed. Later, whenever someone walked by wearing that mask, crows scolded loudly and dove toward it. This kept happening for years. Even more surprising, crows that had never been caught joined in the scolding. Some of them had not even hatched when the first crows were caught.

[3] Crows also solve problems with tools. Some crows poke sticks into holes to pull out bugs. In tests, crows have bent a piece of wire into a hook to lift a small basket of food out of a tube. New Caledonian crows, which live on islands in the Pacific Ocean, are especially skilled with tools.

[4] City crows have found their own tricks. Some have been seen dropping hard nuts onto busy roads. When a car rolls over a nut and cracks it, the crow waits for a break in traffic. Then it flies down to eat.

[5] When a crow dies, other crows often gather around it and call loudly. To a person watching, this can look like a funeral. Some scientists think the crows are studying the scene. They may be learning what to stay away from.
[6] So the next time a crow watches you from a fence, remember that it may be paying close attention. It might even remember you.

sections.heading: Questions 6-10
sections.directions: Use Passage 2, "The Crow Next Door," to answer questions 6-10.

prompt.A: Read paragraph 4 again. After a nut is cracked, the crow waits for a break in traffic before it flies down. What does this detail suggest?
prompt.B: Read paragraph 2 again. Crows that had never been caught also scolded the person in the mask. What does this detail suggest?

A: Crows can tell when a nut has cracked open all the way.
Crows feel safer eating near people than out in the woods.
Crows want to be sure no other crow takes the nut first.
Crows understand that moving cars can hurt them.
B: Crows can learn about danger from other crows.
The crows remembered the person's face from when they were caught.
Crows feel upset when people wear masks to hide their faces.
The crows were likely hungry and wanted food from people.

why.A: D is right. The crow waits for traffic to stop before it flies down, so it knows cars are a danger. The article never compares cities to woods (B). A and C are not why it waits for a break in traffic.
why.B: A is right. Crows that were never caught still scolded the mask, so they learned it from other crows. B is wrong because these crows were never caught. C is wrong because they scolded one certain mask, not every mask. D is not in the article.

questions.skill: Make an inference from an article (Part A)

prompt.A: Part A: What can you infer about the author's view of crows?
prompt.B: Part A: Read paragraph 2. What did the crows most likely believe about the person in the mask?

A: The author likes crows but can find them a little scary.
The author thinks most people do not give crows enough credit.
The author thinks crows should not be allowed to live in cities with people.
The author thinks crows are noisy pests that pick through trash.
B: That it was bringing food to share with them.
That the person was there to help them.
That the person was a threat to crows.
That the person was kind and there to visit them.

why.A: B is right. The author says many people see crows as pests, then shows how smart they are. The author never says crows feel scary (A). C and D are views the author argues against.
why.B: C is right. Crows scolded loudly and dove toward the mask, which is how they act toward danger. A, B and D are friendly ideas, but scolding and diving show the crows saw a threat.

questions.skill: Choose evidence that supports an inference (Part B)

prompt.A: Part B: Which detail BEST supports your answer to Part A?
prompt.B: Part B: Which detail from the article BEST supports your answer to Part A?

A: Crows scolded loudly and dove toward the mask, year after year. (paragraph 2)
Some city crows fly down into busy roads to eat. (paragraph 4)
Many see crows as pests, but they may be very smart. (paragraph 1)
Crows made a lot of noise whenever someone wore the mask. (paragraph 2)
B: The researchers let the crows go unharmed. (paragraph 2)
Researchers wore the mask while catching some crows. (paragraph 2)
Some crows had not even hatched when the first crows were caught. (paragraph 2)
City crows have found their own tricks for getting food on busy roads. (paragraph 4)

why.A: C is right. The author sets the 'pests' view against how smart crows are, which backs Part A choice B. A seems to back 'scary' (Part A choice A). B seems to back crows being trouble in cities (Part A choice C). D seems to back 'noisy pests' (Part A choice D).
why.B: B. Being caught is scary for a crow, and the mask was there each time. That is why crows saw it as a threat. A is about the mask study, but being let go unharmed would not make the mask seem scary. C is about crows learning from others, not why the mask means danger. D is about food, not the mask.

questions.skill: Judge which evidence best proves a claim

prompt.A: A student says, "Crows pass what they know on to other crows." Which detail, if it were the ONLY one you had, would BEST prove this?
prompt.B: A student says, "City crows can plan a few steps ahead." Which detail, if it were the ONLY one you had, would BEST prove this?

A: Scientists have found that city crows may be some of the smartest animals. (paragraph 1)
A crow might even remember you. (paragraph 6)
Crows do not stay quiet when a crow dies; they gather and call. (paragraph 5)
Crows that were not caught joined in scolding the mask. (paragraph 2)
B: A crow drops a nut on a busy road and waits for a break in traffic to eat it. (paragraph 4)
Crows dive at people who once bothered them. (paragraph 2)
Some crows poke sticks into holes to pull out bugs. (paragraph 3)
A crow may watch you from a fence. (paragraph 6)

why.A: D. These crows never met the masked person, so they had to learn about the mask from other crows. B and C sound close but do not prove sharing. B is about one crow remembering, not crows teaching each other. In C, the crows may be studying the scene, but nothing shows them passing anything on. A says crows are smart, not that they share.
why.B: A is right. The crow drops the nut, lets traffic crack it, then waits for a safe time to eat. That is a plan with several steps. C is a one-step tool use. B is memory. D is only watching.

questions.skill: Why the author included a detail (article)

prompt.A: Why does the author say that crows gathering around a dead crow can look like a funeral (paragraph 5)?
prompt.B: Why does the author end the article by saying a crow "might even remember you" (paragraph 6)?

A: To help readers picture the scene with something familiar.
To prove crows feel sad like people.
To show that crows bury their dead under the ground like people.
To show that crows care deeply about the members of their flock.
B: To show that crows like to make friends with the people nearby.
To show that crows enjoy being around people.
To link the face studies to a reader's own daily life.
To prove that crows are the smartest animals around.

why.A: A is right. The author says it 'can look like' a funeral, which compares it to something readers know. Scientists think the crows may be studying the scene, so the article does not claim sadness (B) or deep caring (D). C is not in the article.
why.B: C is right. The ending ties the face studies to a crow on the reader's own fence. The article never says crows make friends with people (A) or enjoy being near them (B). D goes further than the article does.

sections.heading: SHORT RESPONSE (4 points)
sections.directions: Use Passage 1, "Ba-da-bum." Write in complete sentences. Remember C-E-E: Claim, Evidence, Explanation. Check your answer with the rubric before you turn it in.

questions.skill: Constructed response: inference with two pieces of evidence (C-E-E)

prompt.A: Think about how Marisol acts before and after she snaps at Leo. What does this show about her as a person? Use TWO pieces of evidence from the story. Name the paragraph for each one, and explain how it supports your idea.
prompt.B: What can you infer about what kind of person Marisol is? Use TWO pieces of evidence from the story. Name the paragraph for each, and explain how each one proves your idea.

answer.A: Marisol gets tense under pressure, but she is caring and can fix her own mistakes. In paragraph 4 she snaps at Leo and calls his beat wrong, so the stress makes her sharp with him. In paragraphs 6–7 she notices how quiet he has gone, gives him her old practice sticks, and gently shows him how to hold them. That shows she cares about him and wants to make things right after hurting his feelings.
answer.B: Strong answer: Marisol is a caring sister, even when she is stressed. In paragraph 4 she snaps at Leo, but in paragraph 6 she slides her old practice sticks to him. This shows she feels bad and wants to make it right. In paragraph 7 she speaks quietly and tells him he can sit in the front row and watch her hands. This shows she wants him to feel included in her big day. (Other supported inferences are fine, e.g., she is nervous because Abuela will hear her play for the first time, as long as two details really support the claim and are explained.)

why.A: Score with the C-E-E rubric. Look for an inference the story never states outright, two details that each support it, and an explanation of how each detail shows the inference.
why.B: Score with the C-E-E rubric. A retelling of what happens ("She gave Leo the sticks") is a detail, not an inference; the claim must go beyond what the text says.

documents.title: SHORT RESPONSE SELF-CHECK: C-E-E
documents.directions: Before you turn in your short response, read each row. Circle the box that matches your answer. If you are not at a 4 yet, fix your answer first!

rubric.title: What can you infer about the character? (4 points)

criteria.name: Claim (my inference)
levels: I wrote a clear inference about the character. The story does not say it outright. I figured it out from clues.
I wrote an inference, but it is a little unclear or very general.
My claim is close to a detail the story already says.
I only retold what happened, or I made a guess with no clues behind it.

criteria.name: Evidence (proof from the text)
levels: I used TWO pieces of evidence. I named the paragraph or quoted for each one. Each one really proves my inference.
I used two pieces of evidence, but one does not really prove my inference.
I used only one piece of evidence, or I did not say where it came from.
I did not use evidence from the story.

criteria.name: Explanation (how it proves it)
levels: For each piece of evidence, I explained HOW it shows my inference ("This shows that...").
I explained one piece of evidence well, but not the other.
I tried to explain, but I mostly repeated the evidence.
I did not explain how my evidence connects to my inference.

rubric.note: This task is worth 4 points in all. It is not 4 points for each row. Find the level that fits each row. Your score is the level that fits most of your rows (4, 3, 2, or 1). If all three rows are different, your score is the middle one. A 4 means all three parts are strong. A 1 means an inference with no real support, or just retelling the story. Ask yourself: If this were the ONLY sentence I had, would it prove my answer?

wilco.note: rerun after the maker rewrote wrong choices to break the converge cue
rerun after the maker rewrote wrong choices to break the converge cue
after maker round 3: version B failed learnedCV 50%; then, after a learnedCV fix, middle 38% (lead run, not written separately)
after the maker reworded B wrong choices so the key is longest 3, shortest 3, middle 4 times

facts.notes: The crow article holds up against the teacher's notes and published research (the Marzluff/Cornell mask studies, Weir et al. 2002 wire hook, the Sendai nut-dropping crows, Swift & Marzluff 2015 on dead crows). The problems are in the question wording: one evidence choice misstates paragraph 4, one adds a detail to paragraph 3, and one why line claims more than the passage says. Two simplifications go to the teacher. No web search was run; references are from known published studies.

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q9 choice A (key)
findings.what: The choice says the crow 'sets' a nut on the road and 'waits for a car to crack it'. Paragraph 4 says crows drop the nuts, and the waiting it describes comes after the car cracks the nut, when the crow waits for a break in traffic. Reword to match the passage, keeping the same answer.
findings.before: A crow sets a nut on the road and waits for a car to crack it. (paragraph 4)
findings.fixed: Reworded to "A crow drops a nut on a busy road, then waits for a break in traffic to eat it." Same answer, now matches paragraph 4.

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q6 why
findings.what: The explanation says the never-caught crows 'must have learned it from crows that were caught.' The passage only supports learning from other crows (some had not hatched yet, so they may have learned secondhand). Change to 'from other crows.'
findings.source: Passage 2 para 2; Cornell, Marzluff & Pecoraro 2012, Proc. R. Soc. B
findings.fixed: Now says "They must have learned it from other crows."

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q8 choice B
findings.what: The choice says New Caledonian crows live on islands 'far out in' the Pacific; the passage says only 'on islands in the Pacific Ocean,' and the why line calls this detail true. Drop 'far out'.
findings.before: New Caledonian crows live on islands far out in the Pacific Ocean. (paragraph 3)
findings.fixed: The New Caledonian choice was replaced (round 2) with "Some city crows drop hard nuts onto busy roads."

findings.where: Passage 2 para 3 (wire hook sentence)
findings.what: 'In tests, crows have bent a piece of wire into a hook' describes work done mainly with one captive New Caledonian crow (Betty). Because the sentence comes before New Caledonian crows are named, students may think ordinary city crows do this. True as a simplification; the teacher may prefer 'In tests, a New Caledonian crow bent a piece of wire…'

findings.where: Passage 2 para 4 / INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q9 key and why
findings.what: Nut-dropping on roads is well documented (Sendai, Japan), but whether crows use cars on purpose is still debated (a Davis, California study found American crows did not drop more nuts when cars were coming). Inside the passage, the B q9 'plan with several steps' inference is defensible; the teacher may want to keep it as a passage-based inference only.
findings.source: Nihei 1995; Cristol, Switzer, Johnson & Walke 1997, Animal Behaviour

findings.where: all versions
findings.what: I matched 20 of 20 keys without reading either passage, and 17 of those guesses were at confidence 4–5. In most items only the key is about feelings or ideas; the wrong choices are silly literal reasons. Each item needs at least one wrong choice that uses a real passage detail but is not the best inference.
findings.before: e.g. A q1 C/D, A q6 A/C, B q5 A–C
findings.fixed: Partly: in rounds 2 and 3 the maker rewrote wrong choices on all 20 items to use real passage details and believable feelings; passage-free confidence fell from 17 to 15 items at 4–5, but a test-wise reader still matched 20 of 20 (see round 3).

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q4
findings.what: This is a level 3 item, but no wrong choice shows caring, so the key is the only kind act (B is the opposite, A is about Leo, D shows only stress). Change A to a weaker caring detail from paragraph 7, such as 'Marisol tells Leo he can sit in the front row,' which shows kindness but nothing about stress.
findings.before: A. Leo copies the beat Marisol has practiced
findings.fixed: A is now a caring detail from paragraph 7 (front row), so the key is no longer the only kind act.

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q4
findings.what: The key is the only choice that says 'Abuela,' so students can match it to the claim without reading. Change D to an Abuela detail that shows no nerves, such as 'Abuela landed at the airport last night (paragraph 5).' Keep C (shoes), which shows nerves but not why.
findings.before: D. Across the table, Leo taps two spoons
findings.fixed: D now names Abuela (she landed last night) but shows no nerves, so the key is no longer the only Abuela choice.

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q9
findings.what: A level 3 item no harder than level 2: only C competes. Change B to a memory detail that sounds right but is not sharing, such as 'Crows kept scolding the mask for years (paragraph 2).'
findings.before: B. Scientists have been studying city crows
findings.fixed: B and A are now memory and "smart" details that sound right; C (crows gathering) still competes.

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q9
findings.what: The key's wording does not match the passage: paragraph 4 says crows 'drop' nuts, not 'set' them, and it leaves out the clearest planning step. Reword the key with the same meaning ('drops a nut on a busy road, then waits for a break in traffic to eat it'). Also change C to the wire-hook detail from paragraph 3, which shows problem solving but not planning ahead.
findings.before: A. A crow sets a nut on the road and waits for a car to crack it
findings.fixed: The key now says the crow drops the nut and waits for a break in traffic (paragraph 4); C is now a one-step tool detail (round 3).

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q7/q8
findings.what: q8's key says the same thing as q7's key ('people see pests, but smart' = 'don't give enough credit'), so each part gives away the other. The keys can't change, so change q8's wrong choices to details that seem to support q7's wrong choices, e.g. 'Crows scolded loudly and dove toward the mask (paragraph 2),' which seems to support 'crows are a danger.'
findings.before: q8 B. New Caledonian crows live on islands
findings.fixed: Partly: q8 A (scolding the mask) now seems to back q7 A (danger); the key still restates q7's key (see round 2).

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q2/q3
findings.what: Only q3's key fits any Part A answer, so q3 gives q2 away. Change q3 D (about Dad) to a detail that seems to support q2's wrong choice B or C, so students have to answer Part A first.
findings.before: D. Dad slides a plate of eggs toward Marisol
findings.fixed: q3 B (Leo taps spoons) now seems to back Part A choice B (he wants to bug her), so q3 no longer gives q2 away.

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q8
findings.what: A, C and D are all food or tool facts from paragraphs 3–4 and say about the same thing (twin wrong choices), so the key is the odd one out. Replace two of them with mask details that do not show 'threat,' such as 'The crows were let go unharmed (paragraph 2)' and 'Some crows had not even hatched yet (paragraph 2).'
findings.before: A. Crows poke sticks… C. …bend a wire…
findings.fixed: The three twin food/tool choices became two mask details that do not show threat (let go unharmed; not yet hatched) and one road detail.

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ A q11
findings.what: A q4 hands students the inference and the paragraph 6 evidence, and A q1 hands them paragraph 1, so the open item mostly copies earlier items. The stem 'What can you infer about Marisol?' is so broad that a literal fact could pass. Reword it to match B ('…about what kind of person Marisol is'), or aim A q4's claim at a different idea.
findings.before: What can you infer about Marisol?
findings.fixed: Partly: the prompt now asks how Marisol acts before and after she snaps and what that shows about her as a person; A q4 still points to the same evidence (see round 2).

findings.where: INFERENCE AND EVIDENCE QUIZ B q11

notes: Ms. Okafor (made-up sample) ordered a grade 7 ELA quiz with A/B versions on making inferences and citing text evidence, plus a rubric for its short response. The maker wrote two original passages from her lesson notes, a story and an article, and 22 question rows. Three rounds of checks followed, each by agents that had not written the work; every round caught something the round before had missed or created.

Round 1 (14:15–14:40). The maker needed four drafts to get past the lead's pre-checks: on the first draft one test-wise bot (oddOne) picked the key 55% of the time against 25% chance. The fact checker checked 47 claims and flagged 5: 3 to fix and 2 for the teacher. The blind tester first answered all 20 multiple-choice items WITHOUT the passages and matched 20 of 20 keys, 17 at high confidence: a student who skipped the reading could have aced it. Wilco's bots had passed the same quiz at 30%, because the cue was in the content (only the key sounded like a teacher's answer), which the bots can't see. The blind tester listed 11 FIX.

Round 2 (14:44–14:57). A new maker session got only the FIX list and rewrote wrong choices on 18 items, using real details from the passages. Wilco failed it at once: the new wrong choices all borrowed the key's idea, so the 'converge' bot found the key 50% of the time. After a rewording it passed at 31%. A different fresh blind tester confirmed 7 fixes in full and 3 in part, and caught 2 new problems the fixes had created: A q4 and B q9 now had two right answers.

Round 3 (15:00–15:16). A third maker session fixed both two-right items, rewrote one wrong choice on 10 items so a reader who skipped the passage has a believable trap, and rewrote the rubric's scoring note after the lead saw '4 pts' print on every row of a test render (reading as 12 points). Wilco failed twice more (a trained bot at 50% on version B, then the 'middle length' bot at 38%) and passed on the third try at 31%. A third fresh blind tester confirmed the fixes and was the first checker to read the rubric.

Wilco before and after (chance 25%, fail line 35%): maker's first draft oddOne 55% → round 1 pass, posA 30% → round 2 converge 50% → 31% pass → round 3 learnedCV 50% → middle 38% → 31% pass. Answer keys were never changed to pass a bot; one key (B q9) was reworded to match the passage, with the same answer.

Catches in all: 22 FIX findings (fact checker 3, blind testers 11 + 4 + 4). 13 were fully fixed, 4 partly, and 5 are left open for the teacher after the last round: twin wrong choices in B q7, B q10 and A q5, a wording slip in B q3, and a rubric note that contradicts itself. 14 JUDGMENT calls go to the teacher, including the biggest one: three separate blind testers still matched 20 of 20 keys without the passages (17, 17, then 15 at high confidence), mostly because five question stems quote the deciding detail. Fixing that means changing the questions themselves, which is the teacher's call.
This sample stops at the preview, rendered at 15:25 with a watermark. The teacher reads it next and either agrees or asks for changes; nothing final is made without her agreement.

Totals. Wall clock 14:13–15:28, 75 minutes. Agent minutes: 50, or 56 with the lead's logged steps (the lead's relay work between steps is not measured). Cost $7.74, exact, from each agent session's own bill (maker $5.36 over 3 rounds, checkers $1.94, reporter $0.44); the lead's own session is not counted. Tokens as reported: 5,256,800, mostly cache reads, and a floor for the round 3 maker. Per question row (22): about $0.35. Against the menu: 55 tokens = $5.50 of budget, so this first-of-its-kind order ran about $2.24 over at API prices.
